Jeush
jē´ŭsh
n. pr. m. (Hebrew Ye'ush, he will gather, or assembler)
A Hebrew name from a root meaning to gather or hasten to help. The first bearer is a son of Esau and a duke of Edom.

Biblical Definition

Jeush first appears as a son of Esau by his Canaanite wife: “And Aholibamah bare Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah: these are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan” (Gen 36:5). The record is repeated, “and she bare to Esau Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah” (Gen 36:14), and then he is given a title: “And these are the sons of Aholibamah Esau's wife; duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah” (Gen 36:18). The Chronicler repeats the line at the head of his history: “The sons of Esau; Eliphaz, Reuel, and Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah” (1Ch 1:35). Other men bear it: a Benjamite of Bilhan's house (1Ch 7:10), a Levite of the sons of Shimei whose small household was reckoned as one (1Ch 23:11), and a son of Rehoboam whom his father set with his brethren in the fenced cities of Judah (2Ch 11:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) does not treat Scripture proper names; the sense is Hebrew, from a root meaning to gather or to hasten to help.

expand to see more

JEUSH. A Hebrew proper name; from a root signifying to assemble or hasten together.

DUKE, n. In Great Britain, one of the highest order of nobility; in Scripture, the chief of a family or tribe.

GATHER, v.t. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things.

Key Scripture

Gen 36:5 — "And Aholibamah bare Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah: these are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan."

Gen 36:14 — "And these were the sons of Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: and she bare to Esau Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah."

Gen 36:18 — "And these are the sons of Aholibamah Esau's wife; duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah: these were the dukes that came of Aholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife."

1Ch 1:35 — "The sons of Esau; Eliphaz, Reuel, and Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah."

Modern Corruption

Esau's line is treated as an afterthought, while Genesis gives it a full chapter and the New Testament makes it the standing case for election.

expand to see more

Genesis 36 is a whole chapter of dukes, and Jeush is one of them. Esau had lands, cities, chiefs and kings that reigned in Edom before there reigned any king over the children of Israel, while Jacob's house was still a wandering family. Scripture records the prosperity without embarrassment. Worldly success is not evidence of divine favour, and Genesis proves it by giving the rejected brother the more impressive genealogy.

Paul takes exactly this material for the sharpest statement of unconditional election in the canon: the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, it was said, The elder shall serve the younger. As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated. The dukes of Edom are not an interruption in the covenant story; they are the visible half of the doctrine, and the doctrine is that God's choice does not answer to what men can see.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Ye'ush (H3266), assembler; 'alluph (H441), duke or chief of a clan; 'Edom (H123), red, the nation of Esau.

expand to see more

Hebrew Ye'ush (H3266) — Jeush; Genesis 36:5, 36:14, 1 Chronicles 1:35.

Hebrew 'alluph (H441) — duke, chief; the title given him in Genesis 36:18.

Hebrew 'Oholibamah (H173) — Aholibamah, his mother, Esau's Canaanite wife.

Hebrew 'Esav (H6215) — Esau; the brother whose line Genesis 36 records.

Hebrew 'Edom (H123) — Edom, red; the nation descended from him.

Usage

"“These are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan” — and Genesis names them all."

"“Duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah” — titles Jacob's sons did not yet have."

"A chapter of Edomite nobility, recorded without envy and without approval."
